newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline prices fall on Iraq promise to halt attacks.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline prices fall on Iraq promise to halt attacks.

text.p: Gasoline prices fell Friday after Iraq said it would halt attacks on U.S. warplanes patrolling "no-fly zones" in Iraq, reversing a rally to near post-Gulf War highs on jitters about U.S. military stikes.

Sugar prices slid after a bearish production report from the U.S. government. Corn and soybean prices tumbled after private forecasters lessened the chance for a crop-damaging freeze later this month.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange gasoline prices rose early Friday amid expectations of an imminent U.S. attack against Iraq. Prices swiftly fell after Baghdad said it would halt attacks on U.S. warplanes flying in the no-fly zones.
Iraq's statements implied an easing of tensions and a lessening of threats to the vital Mideast oil supply. However, traders and analysts said further price fluctuations were likely.

"The problem is that Saudi Arabia is about the only oil producer who has spare capacity, so any tension in that area is likely to keep prices firm," said Bob Finch, head of trading in London at oil trading and refining company Vito SA.

NYMEX gasoline for October delivery fell 131 cents at 64.60 cents per gallon and October crude oil was down 49 cents at $24.51 per barrel. October heating oil was off 1.23 cents at 67.94 cents per gallon.
A bearish production report coupled with bearish action in the sugar options market fuelled selling in New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange sugar futures.
The U.S. Agriculture Department estimated world sugar output at 121.4 million metric tons, up from a May estimate of 120.2 million. Production estimates for India and Brazil were also raised.
Also, expiration of CSCE options on the October sugar futures was bearish. Traders said many October options traded at the equivalent of an 11.50-cent October futures price.
The CSCE October contract closed down 0.25 cent at 11.64 cents per pound.
CBOT corn and soybean futures fell as fears about frost damage to the U.S. crops eased.
"We're just putting weather premium in, then taking it out ... back and forth," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
Corn and soybeans prices had risen Thursday after a private weather forecaster said there was a large chance for a crop-damaging frost for Sept. 23 or 24 in northern areas of the U.S. Midwest.
Early Friday weather maps indicated diminished concern about cold weather soon in the leading U.S. corn and soybean states.
"Today's version (of the maps) does not infer a freeze on the (Sept.) 23 or 24," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster for Weather Express Inc.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, December corn closed down 8-1/2 cents at $3.21-1/2 per bushel and November soybeans were off 12-1/2 cents at $8.02 per bushel.
